div.p: In this paper we study and model the schedulability problem for multi-core real-time systems using an extended task automata, which was first proposed as an event-driven task model for real time systems with non-uniformly recurring computation tasks. Original task automata allow only one calculation unit to process tasks, i.e. on a single-core processor. With the extension presented in this paper, we eliminate this restriction and allow more calculation units, i.e. on a multi-core processor. The most significant application of this extension is in the analysis of schedulability on a multi-core processor with implicit task migration. We use task automata to model the non-deterministic arrival times of tasks. Schedulability problem is to check whether all the released tasks may finish within their deadlines on multicore systems. We shall show that schedulability of a multi-core task automaton is decidable under such circumstances as (1) task feedback is not allowed, (2)task execution time is fixed, i.e. best and worst execution time are equal.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems typically consist of a set of real-time tasks and a scheduling strategy, which is implemented as a scheduler. The scheduler, i.e. scheduling strategy, is a critical component of real-time systems. It makes the decision in which order and on which hardware the released tasks are to be executed, based on task properties and the system state. Schedulability analysis is to analyze whether all the released tasks can finish execution within their deadlines. In recent years, task automata have been applied to modelling task release patterns and solving the problem for single-processor systems successfully.

In [2], task automata are an extension to timed automata with tasks. Compared with other classic task models on scheduling, it is more expressive for modeling dynamic and non-deterministic task releases and preemptions. It is shown that for a large classes of single-core systems, the problem can be solved automatically using algorithmic methods.

We assume that the system has a central processing unit with a fixed number of cores. Core is the minimum calculation unit. There could be no more than one task running on each core and no task could occupy more than one core at a time. Further we assume the cost of task migration between cores is low enough to be neglectable.

In this paper, we shall model preemptive schedulers based on task automata in the multi-core settings. Compared with models in [3], our model allows task migration between cores implicitly, which is an effective way to improve response time. This paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the syntax and semantics of the task automata. Formal schedulability is given in section III. Preemptive scheduler modeling and analysis on multi-core processors is presented in section IV. Section V concludes this paper.
Due to the lack of space, we omit proofs of lemmas and theorems, which can be found on my homepage.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY
div.p: In this section, we'll study schedulability. We assume here that any running task can be preempted at any time. We use q err to denote a task queue where a task instance p(w, d) has missed its deadline, i.e. d < 0.

div.head: Definition 6 (Schedulability). A task automaton
div.p: A with an initial state (l 0 , u 0 , q 0 ) is non-schedulable with Sch if (l 0 , u 0 , q 0 ) → * (l, u, q err ) for some l and u. Otherwise, we say that A is schedulable with Sch. More generally, we say that A is schedulable if and only if there exists a scheduling strategy Sch with which A is schedulable.

div.head: IV. MODELLING AND ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section we shall model preemptive schedulers on multi-core processors.
We shall consider such automata as completion time of a task does not influence the release of another task instance, i.e. with no task feedback.

div.head: A. Ideas
div.p: We use p ij to denote a task instance of ith task type in the task queue, where j is some index that is not in use by any other task instance of task type P i in the queue. Whenever task instance p ij finishes, j is reused. Thus we can distinguish a task instance from other task instances of the same task type. Note that indices i and j are both bounded, the former by the number of task types, the latter by the maximal number of task instances of ith task type in the task queue.

We encode task preemptions using subtraction on clocks. To track the remaining computation time, relative deadline and the preemption time, we introduce three clocks for each task instance p ij : x c ij (a computing clock) remembers the accumulated computation time since p ij is started, x d ij (a deadline clock) remembers the deadline and it is reset to 0 when p ij is released and x p ij (a preemption clock) remembers the time since p ij is preempted or released and it is reset to 0 when p ij is preempted or released.

On a multi-core processor, we use a clock x p ij to track the duration the task instance p ij is preempted. It is reset whenever p ij is preempted. When task p ij is scheduled to run again, the remaining execution time is v(
div.formula: x c ij ) -v(x p ij ). Note that x p ij is bounded by D i . When task p ij is preempted, D i ≥ 0, v(x p ij ) = 0 and v(x c ij ) ≥ 0, so Di ≥ v(x c ij ) ≥ v(x p ij ). As time progresses, the invariant D i ≥ v(x c ij ) ≥ v(x p ij
div.p: ) still holds, otherwise this task instance misses its deadline and the task queue turns into an error queue. So when task p ij is scheduled to run again, v(x c ij )v(x p ij ) is strictly nonnegative and v(x p ij ) is not more than D i . Thus we can encode preemptive schedulers using timed automata with bounded subtraction.

Assume a task automaton A on tasks with fixed computation times, and a preemptive scheduling strategy Sch s . Let E(A) denote the timed automaton of A, where actions labels on each edges leading to a node which maps to a task type P i are replaced with release i . For the preemptive scheduling strategy Sch s , we construct E(Sch s ) as a timed automaton with bounded subtraction, synchronized with E(A) through the release i s. Locations in this automaton encode the queues from all the possible adequate states except an Err location, where the task queue is an error queue in general, and edges denote the scheduling strategy and the rules for task finishing.

div.head: B. Utilities
div.p: To easily track the status of each task instance in the task queue, we add a variable Status(ij) for each p ij , which is initialized to free. Each task instance p ij has one of the following status: free means task instance p ij is finished or not released yet, ready means task instance p ij is released or preempted, and ready to run and running means task instance p ij is running.
Note that as in our model, we see no difference between a preempted task and a released-but-has-never-run task when calculating the remaining computation time. So we treat them the same way.
We use locations to remember which task instances are running at the moment. E(Sch s ) has the following types of locations:

1) Idling means the task queue is empty, i.e. Status(ij)=free for all i, j, 2) Running(i 1 j 1 , . . . , i k j k ) means k task instances p i1j1 , . . . , p i k j k are running on k cores independently where 0 < k < s, i.e. for all ij in (i 1 j 1 , . . . , i k j k ), Status(ij)=running and for all ij not in (i 1 j 1 , . . . , i k j k ), Status(ij)=free 3) Running(i 1 j 1 , . . . , i s j s ) means s task instances p i1j1 , . . . , p isjs are running on s cores, and for all ij in p i1j1 , . . . , p isjs , Status(ij)=running, and for all ij in p i1j1 , . . . , p isjs , it has invariant x c ij ≤ W i , and x d kl ≤ D k for all k, l such that Status(kl) =free. Note here that the third type is different from the second type in that there is no other task waiting to be scheduled to run.

In order to keep track of the order of task instances in E(Sch s ), we use a variable Position(ij) for each task p ij , which is initialized to -1 for all p ij , Status(ij)=free or set to the index for all p ij , Status(ij) = free. As on multi-core processors the first s tasks are executing, the positions of running tasks range from 1 to s, i.e. Position(ij) ∈ (1, 2, . . . , s)
if Status(ij)=running. Since the length of the task queue is bounded at any time point, Position(ij) is finite for all p ij .

div.head: C. Predicates
div.p: When a task finishes or a new task arrives, we need to update the positions of each task instance whose status is not free. We define the following predicates to assist updates:

• Next(mn) denotes that the task instance p mn is the next task instance to execute. Newly released task instance is also taken into account. • Remove(mn) denotes the removal of the task instance p mn from the task queue and the update of the variables Positions(ij) for all p ij . • Insert(mn) denotes the insertion of a new task instance p mn into the task queue according to the scheduling strategy and the update of the variables Positions(ij) for all p ij including p mn . • Last(mn) denotes that the task instance p mn is the last running task in the queue. These predicates can be encoded using timed automata guards on the values w ij , d ij of the task instances, which can be reconstructed from the clocks x c ij , x d ij , x p ij . Take EDF (Earliest Deadline First) as an example. Assume on a two-core system, there are three tasks in the task queue in order, namely, p ab , p cd and p ef . The first two tasks are running, p ef is waiting and p gh will be released. mn is a place-holder of ab, cd and ef .
div.formula: • Next(ef ) is true if x c ab = W a or x c cd = W c . • Next(gh) is true if D g < D a -x d ab or D g < D c -x d
if D g < D r -x d r1 and D g >= D l -x d l1 . • Last(mn) is true if ∀p ij ∈ q and Status(ij)=running, D m -x d mn >= D i -x i ij .

div.head: F. Adding Error location
div.p: To detect whether a non-adequate state is reachable in A Schs , we add a location Err and edges to E(Sch s ) as follows:

1) Running(i 1 j 1 , . . . , i l j l ) to Err: guard: for some mn ∈ (i 1 j 1 , . . . , i l j l ), x c mn < W m , and x d mn = D m action: none reset: none 2) Running(i 1 j 1 , . . . , i l j l ) to Err: for each k, l, there is an edge labeled with guard: Status(kl)=ready, x d kl = D k action: none reset: none 3) Running(i 1 j 1 , . . . , i l j l ) to Err: for each k, there is an edge labeled with guard: Status(kl) = free for all l action: release k reset: none

div.p: We show a concise example of E(Sch s ) in Fig 1 . It models a scheduler on a two-core processor. We assume the corresponding E(A) releases only one tasks of type P (3, 3) and 4 task instances will make the queue overflow for simplicity. As there are many edges betweeen locations, we present one edge of each kind with the number of such edges marked on the circle. In the figure, c1 refers to clock x c 11 , d1 to x d 11 and p1 to x p 11 . Run1 is the counterpart of Running(ij), and Run2 of Running(i 1 j 1 , ..., i s j s ).
Note that the number of edges is bounded by the number of cores, task types, and task instances of each type.

div.head: H. Decidability
div.p: Let v 0 be a clock valuation which assigns zero to all clocks of the scheduler automaton E(Sch s ). Lemma 3. Let A be a task automaton with tasks whose computation time is fixed and Sch s a preemptive scheduling strategy. Assume that (l 0 , u 0 , q 0 ) and ((l 0 , Idling), u 0 ∪ v 0 ) are the initial states of A and the product automaton E(A) E(Sch s ), respectively. Then 1) if there are l and u such that (l 0 , u 0 , q 0 → * (l, u, q err ) then ((l 0 , Idling), u 0 ∪ v 0 ) → * ((l , Err), u ∪ v) for some l , u , and v, and 2) if there are l and u, and v such that ((l 0 , Idling), u 0 ∪ v 0 ) → * ((l , Err), u ∪ v) then (l 0 , u 0 , q 0 ) → * (l, u, q err ) for some l , u . Now we have the correctness lemma for our encoding, and the lemma 3 showing that the multi-core schedulability analysis problem can be solved by reachability analysis for timed automata extended with subtraction. From Lemma 2, E(Sch s ) is bounded.

Theorem 1. The problem of checking schedulability relative to a preemptive scheduling strategy with multi-core processors is decidable for task automata with fixed computation times. Proof: This theorem follows from Lemma 1, 2, and 3.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: We modeled preemptive scheduling strategies on multi-core platforms and proved its correctness. The problem of checking schedulability on it is reduced to be a reachability problem on timed automata and is proved to be decidable. This model assumes all the cores share the same calculation capacity, thus does not distinguish on which core the task is running. Further, our model schedules tasks to an abstract layer, a queue for all cores, instead of to the physical core, whereby it can treat all tasks equally across cores, allowing task migration whenever needed.
